analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 30% minimum tax on incomes above one million dollars.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 1, 2025, and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, where it has sat with no markup or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a second, minimum tax: any household earning more than $1 million a year would pay at least 30% of its income in federal taxes, with charitable giving as the only deduction allowed to reduce that floor. Taxes already paid, including Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, would count toward the 30%, and the tax would phase in gradually to avoid a sudden jump for people just over the line. It takes effect for tax years after 2024 and the $1 million threshold would rise with inflation. A separate section states the House's view that this should be an interim step toward broader tax reform that closes loopholes for the wealthiest taxpayers [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers whose share of the tax burden would shrink as millionaires pay more, and every holder of the federal debt, since the bill's stated purpose is to raise tens of billions a year and cut the deficit [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Middle-class taxpayers and federal deficit reduction

how_it_helps.text: It guarantees that taxpayers with income above $1 million pay at least 30% of their adjusted gross income in federal taxes, closing the gap that lets some very high earners pay lower effective rates than middle-income families by claiming deductions and benefiting from lower rates on investment income [S2].

Taxes already paid, including the employee payroll taxes for Social Security and Medicare and the net investment income tax, count toward the 30% floor, so no one would pay the minimum tax purely on top of what they already owe [S2].

The bill phases in gradually, so a household just over $1 million does not face a sudden jump: the tax applies only to the share of income above the threshold, scaled by how far over it the taxpayer is [S2].
A 'sense of the House' section in the bill states it would cut the deficit by billions of dollars a year and serve as a floor on taxes for the highest-income taxpayers ahead of broader reform [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The small fraction of tax filers with annual income above $1 million, whose preferential rates on investment gains, pass-through business income, and large itemized deductions could no longer push their effective rate below 30% [S2].

drawbacks.text: The floor is computed on adjusted gross income with only charitable giving allowed as a deduction, which means common deductions for state taxes, mortgage interest, and business expenses would no longer reduce a millionaire's minimum tax [S2].

A 30% floor on a single year's income can be hard on taxpayers with volatile income, such as a business owner who sells a company once after years of losses, since the tax is based on that year's adjusted gross income rather than average earnings [S2].
The bill creates a second, parallel tax calculation on top of the regular income tax and the existing alternative minimum tax, adding complexity for high-income filers and their preparers [S2].

The bill text does not include a formal revenue estimate, so the claim that it cuts the deficit by billions a year appears only in the 'sense of the House' section rather than in a scored figure [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is straightforward fairness: it stops the very highest earners from paying lower effective rates than ordinary families and raises revenue from the people best able to pay it, while the phase-in and payroll-tax credit blunt the harshest edges. The real costs fall on a small group, but two design questions are legitimate: taxing a single year's income at a 30% floor can overtax people with one-time windfalls, and allowing only charitable deductions narrows the tax code for a group that currently plans around deductions for state taxes and business costs. On balance the costs are narrow and the stated goal, deficit reduction of billions a year, is real if the estimate holds.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and no markup, hearing, or floor vote has followed.

narrative.text: Rep. Brendan Boyle of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on April 1, 2025, joined by Rep. Ro Khanna and Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton as original cosponsors [S2].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that handles tax legislation [S4].
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action [S4].

The bill would take effect for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, meaning any revenue forgone while it sits in committee is revenue that high-income households continue to shield under current law [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households that benefit from current preferential rates and large deductions are better off so far, because the bill has not advanced and the current tax treatment they rely on remains in place. Deficit reduction that the bill says it would deliver has not happened.

for.name: Rep. Brendan F. Boyle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to set a 30% minimum tax on incomes above $1 million.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to committee and has not scheduled a hearing or markup; the action history shows nothing beyond the referral.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes exist yet; every sponsor and cosponsor is a Democrat (Boyle, Khanna, Norton), and Republicans hold a 223-seat House majority, so the bill's fate currently rests with the opposing party.

industries.industry: Households earning over $1 million a year
industries.note: The bill caps how low their effective tax rate can go, disallowing most deductions from the 30% floor and ending the ability of very high earners to pay rates at or below middle-income families' rates [S2].

industries.industry: Private equity, hedge fund, and pass-through business owners
industries.note: Income from carried interest and pass-through businesses flows into adjusted gross income, so the 30% floor would claw back the benefit of lower rates on that income [S2].

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax planning services for high earners
industries.note: The bill adds a second parallel tax calculation, creating both compliance work and new planning questions for clients near the $1 million threshold [S2].

analysis.trajectory: Very unlikely to advance. The bill has had no movement since its April 2025 referral, Republicans control the House, Senate, and the White House, and similar minimum-tax proposals in past Congresses died in the Ways and Means Committee. Its realistic path is reintroduction in a future Congress if control flips.
